title: Dissociation: detaching when something is overwhelming
description: A reminder of something traumatic, or stress that is too much, and instead of a surge of feeling there is distance: feeling unreal, detached, numb. The leading account is that the brain's regulating regions clamp down too hard on the emotional ones. It is the opposite pattern to being flooded by emotion, where those same regulating regions do too little. There is no "typical response" to compare with, because this is one of two different responses to the same kind of trigger.
caveat: The clamp-down account comes mainly from small studies of people with post-traumatic stress disorder listening to accounts of their own trauma, summarised in one review. It is a proposal: more activity in regulating regions alongside less in emotional ones is consistent with suppression, but that does not prove one causes the other. A later systematic review concluded that dissociation cannot be pinned to a few regions and differs with the kind of symptoms, and a pilot study in borderline personality disorder found the insula more active with dissociation, not less. How an episode ends has not been studied; the last phase is an assumption. Dissociation in borderline personality disorder may not match the pattern found in trauma studies.

phases.name: Too much
phases.caption: A reminder of something traumatic, or stress that is overwhelming. In the studies behind this episode, people listened to an account of their own trauma.

phases.name: Clamping down
phases.caption: Regions that regulate arousal and emotion, the medial prefrontal cortex and the dorsal anterior cingulate, become unusually active.

order.rationale: The studies compare whole periods of listening to a trauma account with a neutral one. That the regulating regions rise first and the emotional regions fall second is the logic of the suppression account, not something timed.

phases.name: Detached
phases.caption: Feeling drops away. The more active the medial prefrontal cortex, the less active the amygdala; the stronger the detachment, the quieter the front of the right insula, which normally carries the felt state of the body. Pain is felt less.

order.rationale: The quieter emotional regions are measured over the same period as the more active regulating regions, as correlations. Showing them as a later step follows the suppression account.

phases.name: Easing
phases.caption: The detachment eases. How this happens in the brain, and how long it takes, has not been studied; this last part is an assumption.

order.rationale: No source read for this episode followed the end of a dissociative state. The return towards baseline is assumed.

regions.explanation: Unusually active in people with the dissociative form of post-traumatic stress disorder, and more active the stronger the dissociative response. A systematic review across diagnoses also lists the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex among the regions that mark dissociation. Another review found that dissociation cannot be tied to a few regions.

regions.explanation: In one study of people with post-traumatic stress after road accidents, the more active the dissociation-related part of the medial prefrontal cortex was, the less active the amygdala. This is read as the regulating regions suppressing the emotional ones, which is an interpretation. The opposite pattern, too little regulation, is found in people who are flooded by the memory instead.
